Kinrei-tsuka Kofun Kofun
Part of the remaining posterior circular mound {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=14|frame-width=270}} | location=Nagazuka, {{ill|Kisarazu, Chiba|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}} | Position={{coord|35|23|14|N|139|55|58|E|scale:10000}} | Shape=Keyhole-shaped kofun | Dimensions=Addrox. 100 meters in length; including double moats, addrox. 140 meters in total length | BurialFacility=No-sleeve horizontal stone chamber, green schist stone sarcophagus, and wooden coffin | ConstructionEra=Late 6th century to early 7th century | BuriedPerson={{ill|Makuta Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|馬来田国造}}? | DesignatedCulturalProperty=Prefectural Historic Site | ExcavatedArtifacts=5 pure gold bells, 17 {{ill|Ornamental swords|ja|装飾付大刀}}, gilt bronze horse gear, gilt bronze ceremonial footwear, gilt bronze earrings, amber beads, {{ill|agate|ja|メノウ}} magatama, crystal beads, glass beads, mirrors, bronze bowls, iron spears, iron arrowheads, {{ill|haji ware|ja|土師器}}, and {{ill|sue ware|ja|須恵器}} | DesignationOfArtifacts=Excavated artifacts and stone sarcophagus designated as Important Cultural Property | Map2={{location map|Japan Chiba|lat_deg=35|lat_min=23|lat_sec=14|lon_deg=139|lon_min=55|lon_sec=58|label=Kinrei-tsuka Kofun|mark=前方後円墳-西南西.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kinrei-tsuka Kofun''' (金鈴塚古墳) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}} located in Nagazuka, {{ill|Kisarazu, Chiba|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}, and is part of the {{ill|Gion-Nagazuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}The Gion-Nagazuka Kofun Group is also referred to as the Gion Kofun Group or the Kisarazu Kofun Group. This article adopts the terminology used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007).. == Overview == {{Japanese Kofun |Name = Kinreizuka Kofun |image = [[File:Kinreizuka-1.jpg|250px]]
Kinreizuka Kofun Mound
A portion of the rear circular mound still remains {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=14|frame-width=270}} |Location = {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}{{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}{{ill|Nagasuka|ja|長須賀}} |Coordinates = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|23|14|N|139|55|58|E|scale:10000}} |Shape = {{ill|Keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}} |Scale = Overall mound length [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m; including its double moats, about 140 m in total |Burial facility = Sleeve‐less horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber; stone coffin made of green mud slate and a wooden coffin |Construction period = Late 6th century – Early 7th century |Interred = {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}? |Designated Cultural Property = Prefectural Historic Site |Excavated items = 5 pure–gold bells, {{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}} × 17, bronze–made horse fittings, bronze–made decorative shoes, bronze–made ear rings, an amber jujube bead, {{ill|Agate|ja|メノウ|lt=Agate magatama|lt_ja=製勾玉}}, a crystal–faceted bead, a glass bead, a mirror, a bronze vessel, an iron spear, an iron arrowhead, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土師器}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}} |Excavated items designation = The excavated items and the stone coffin have been designated as Important Cultural Properties |Map 2 = {{Location map|Japan Chiba|lat_deg=35|lat_min=23|lat_sec=14|lon_deg=139|lon_min=55|lon_sec=58|label=Kinreizuka Kofun|mark=前方後円墳-西南西.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kinreizuka Kofun''' (金鈴塚古墳) is a keyhole‐shaped kofun belonging to the {{ill|Gion‐Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}Although the group is sometimes referred to as the Gion Kofun Group or the Kisarazu Kofun Group, here the name “Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group” as used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007) is adopted. and is located in Nagasuka of {{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}. It is a keyhole‐shaped kofun. == Overview == Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole‐shaped mound with an overall length of [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m. It was once known as Nikoizuka Kofun; however, during excavations in [[1950]], five gold bells along with many other valuable artifacts were unearthed from its previously unrobbed horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, and the mound was subsequently renamed Kinreizuka Kofun in reference to the gold bells. Based on the nature of the excavated items, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered to have been constructed during the final phase of keyhole–shaped kofun, in the late 6th to early 7th century. The interred individual is believed to have been a chieftain of the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}} basin, with some attributing the identity to {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. As one of the largest keyhole–shaped kofun from the final phase, and with parts of its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber built using shaped stone, the structure employed innovative construction techniques for its time. The abundant excavated artifacts – including the gold bells and the stone coffin – were recognized for their scholarly importance and were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Furthermore, the remaining mound was designated as a Prefectural Historic Site on November 3, 1950. == Location == Kinreizuka Kofun is situated on an alluvial plain formed by the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}}, at an elevation of about 5.5 m above sea level. The plain once featured several low ridges – formerly sand dunes – and Kinreizuka Kofun was built on one such elevated spot relative to its surroundings武田（1951）dd.10-16. The area around the kofun consists of low–lying, moist land that was once mainly used for rice paddies and lotus fields; as a result, the mound eventually became utilized for land reclamation in these low–lying areas武田（1951）p.3、安藤（1998）p.14. By the end of the Meiji period the mound was recognized as a kofun and was known as Nikoizuka Kofun. At that time a small shrine venerating the kofun’s proprietor was erected on the mound by its landowner千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3. However, examination of a cadastral map drawn in April [[1876]] revealed that part of Kinreizuka Kofun had already been converted to farmland, and by the early Meiji period its original form was beginning to deteriorate武田（1951）dd.16-17. Continued land reclamation in the surrounding lowlands eventually caused most of the mound to disaddear, so that by the time of the 1950 excavation, its anterior part had almost vanished – rendering it almost circular and obscuring its original shape. After the 1950 excavation, urban development in Kisarazu further eroded the mound; the entire anterior section and part of the rear circular portion have since disaddeared, leaving only a remnant of the rear circular mound around the stone chamber, with the remainder largely replaced by residential areas. == The Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group and Kinreizuka Kofun == The {{ill|Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}, to which Kinreizuka Kofun belongs, is believed to have begun its kofun construction in the early to mid–5th century in the lower Kobiki River basin小沢（2007）p.141、白石（2007）dd.dd6-dd7. The earliest kofun in the group is estimated to be the {{ill|Takanagayachōshizuka Kofun|ja|高柳銚子塚古墳}}, with an estimated length of about 130 m; although construction paused from the late 5th to early 6th century, kofun continued to be built until the mid–7th century小沢（2007）p.141. Within this group, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as having been constructed as the last keyhole–shaped kofun during the late 6th to early 7th century. By that time, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun was drawing to a close nationwide, making Kinreizuka Kofun one of the final examples白石（2007）p.141. Within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group, a hierarchical structure existed – with large mounds about 100 m in length like Kinreizuka Kofun alongside somewhat smaller keyhole–shaped and round kofun. Thus, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered one of the chief (leader) mounds of the group. As a kofun constructed roughly contemporaneously with Kinreizuka Kofun, the {{ill|Maruyama Kofun|ja|丸山古墳}}, a keyhole–shaped mound about 70 m in length located [[Category:pp error]]approximately 700 m to the northeast, is often cited小沢（2007）p.148、小沢（2008）dd.373-374. Incidentally, after Kinreizuka Kofun was built, it is believed that a square kofun – the {{ill|Matsumen Kofun|ja|松面古墳}} – was constructed within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. The shift from keyhole–shaped to square kofun after the end of keyhole–shaped kofun construction is a trait also seen in prominent kofun groups of the Kanto region such as the {{ill|Uchizuka Kofun Group|ja|内裏塚古墳群}} in the lower reaches of the {{ill|Koito River|ja|小糸川}} in {{ill|Futtsu City|ja|富津市}} and the {{ill|Saitama Kofun Group|ja|埼玉古墳群}}. == Structure == [[File:Kinreizuka-2.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone chamber of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Based on aerial photographs taken by the US military in [[1946]], excavation results from [[1950]], and boundary surveys conducted during nearby construction from [[1998]] to [[2003]], it has been clarified that Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole–shaped mound [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m in length, with its anterior (front) portion on the west and its rear circular portion on the east. The mound is surrounded by a double moat, giving it an overall length of about 140 m木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.2、酒巻（2000）p.149. The inner moat is estimated to be about 1 m deep, while the outer moat is somewhat shallower安藤（1998）p.18. Although the mound currently stands at about 3.5 m in height, the 1950 excavation report estimated that it originally reached around 6 m based on the sediment that had flowed into the stone chamber; thus, its mound height was relatively low compared to its area武田（1951）dd.22-23、小沢（2008）p.309. Its form is thought to be two–tiered – a common feature in later–period kofun – with the first tier being relatively low with a gentle slope or serving as a platform稲木（2006）p.58. In the rear circular portion there is a horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber constructed of {{ill|Sandstone|ja|砂岩}} quarried in the Futtsu area, with its entrance facing south. The entrance opens on the second tier of the mound. The stone chamber is of the sleeve–less type, indistinguishable from its passage (【羨道】), and was restored in [[1951]] based on the 1950 excavation; its current dimensions are [[Category:pp error]]approximately 9.6 m in length, 2.2 m at its maximum width, and 2 m in height. The chamber’s profile widens gradually from its somewhat narrow entrance, then narrows slightly from the floor toward the ceiling, where a large capstone is set. However, because the entrance was cut away during road construction in [[1932]], the original precise configuration of the chamber remains unknown武田（1950）dd.25-31. Its design follows the traditional style of horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers seen in keyhole–shaped kofun in southwestern Kazusa, such as those in the Uchizuka Kofun Group in Futtsu City; yet, similarities are noted between its chamber and that of the [[Sengenyama Kofun (Sakae)|Sengenyama Kofun]] of the Ryūkakudera Kofun Group in [[Sakae, Imba District|Sakae]], Chiba – suggesting that a standardized style may have been employed in stone chamber construction in late–period keyhole–shaped kofun in the Bōsō region小沢（2008）、p.373 白井（2009)dd.21-25. == History of the Excavation == [[File:Kinreizuka-3.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone coffin of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Plans for excavating Kinreizuka Kofun had been considered since the Taishō period; however, around 1932Some sources date this to 1933 (e.g., 小沢（2008）p.398). Here, the report by the landowner published in the Chiba Prefectural Board of Education (1951) dd.17-18 is followed, dating it to around 1932. a road was built that cut into part of the remaining rear circular mound. During this construction the entrance to the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber was also cut away, leading to the discovery of bronze decorative shoes and other artifacts. Many of the major items were donated by the landowner and collected by the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}, though some materials were lost千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3、酒巻（2007）dd.10-12. After the road construction, as the mound continued to be eroded and parts of the stone chamber became exposed—raising the risk of looting—local archaeologists called for the preservation and excavation of the kofun in March 1950. Consequently, the Chiba Prefectural Historic Sites Investigation Committee, together with the Archaeological Research Laboratory of {{ill|Waseda University|ja|早稲田大学}}, conducted an excavation from April 15 to 19, 1950. When excavation began, the disaddearance and collapse of the chamber’s capstone had resulted in the interior being completely filled with sediment, so excavation was carried out from the udder part of the chamber rather than from its entrance. However, due to the unexpectedly large remaining capstone, progress was slow; the central portion of the chamber and the interior of the stone coffin were excavated first, with the remainder to be tackled later. A second excavation survey of the stone chamber was conducted from July 25 to 31, 1950, during which both the passageway at the entrance and the rear section were investigated千葉県社会教育課（1951）dd.3-7. As a result of these two rounds of excavation, an abundance of burial goods was discovered within the previously untouched stone chamber. During the July phase, five gold bells were found at the innermost part; in reference to these bells, on November 3, 1950, the kofun was designated as a historic site by Chiba Prefecture and renamed from Nikoizuka Kofun to Kinreizuka Kofun木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.4. Subsequently, during reconstruction work near the kofun in 1998, a boundary survey was conducted to ascertain its scale, and from 2000 to 2003 trenches were dug around it for further confirmation. Then, from July 28 to August 8, 2003, the remaining portion of the rear circular mound was surveyed and the stone chamber was re-excavated. These surveys confirmed that the mound measures about 100 m in length ([[Category:pp error]]approximately 140 m including its double moats) and revealed that parts of the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber were constructed using shaped stone – notably with cut stone laid on the floor – demonstrating advanced construction techniques for its time戸倉（2004）dd.32-34、41. == Excavated Items == No haniwa were found to have been used in Kinreizuka Kofun, suggesting that haniwa were not employed in its construction白石（2007）p.143; this further suddorts its classification as a late keyhole–shaped kofun. An enormous quantity of artifacts was recovered from the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber. During the 1950 excavation it was confirmed that at least three bodies were interred within the chamber – one in the central part of the stone coffin, one at its rear, and one at its front. Based on the assemblage of artifacts, it is deduced that the body at the rear of the stone coffin was interred first, followed by the one inside, and finally the body at the front. Although two pairs of ear rings were recovered from the front—suggesting that two individuals may originally have been interred there—there is no decisive evidence for multiple burials in the central and rear portions. Moreover, the relatively undisturbed state of the burial goods implies that repeated secondary interments are unlikely, and it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 4–5 individuals were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun小沢（2008）dd.309-310. From the rear of the stone coffin were unearthed the gold bells (from which the kofun takes its name), amber jujube beads, glass beads, a bronze crown, a mirror, a bronze vessel, bronze horse fittings, an iron spear, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword ({{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}}), and a large quantity of {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}}. The discovery of iron nails from the rear suggests that the body was interred in a wooden coffin. In addition[[Category:addition]], from within the stone coffin a mirror, bronze vessel, armor, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword, and bronze ear rings and glass beads were recovered, while bronze horse fittings found adjacent to the coffin are regarded as the burial goods of the interred individual. Skeletal analysis indicates that the individual in the stone coffin was a young adult male. Furthermore, from the front of the stone coffin were recovered codder vessels, bronze horse fittings, a decorated sword, crystal–faceted beads, and glass beads; bronze decorative shoes unearthed during the 1932 road construction are also considered to be associated with the individual interred at the front. The recovery of iron nails from the front confirms that this individual, too, was interred in a wooden coffin白石（2007）dd.122-127、杉山（1999）p.75. The stylistic features of the Sue pottery and decorated sword, the absence of haniwa on the mound, and the use of cut stone in parts of the chamber all indicate that Kinreizuka Kofun was constructed in the late 6th to early 7th century金鈴塚古墳の造営時期については、小沢（2008）らは6世紀末、白石（2007）は7世紀初頭とする. Furthermore, the Sue pottery exhibits a wide range of manufacturing dates酒巻（2006）によれば、金鈴塚古墳石室内で発見された須恵器の多くは6世紀末から7世紀初めのものであったが、その後に出現したタイプの須恵器も出土しており、7世紀後半に出現した須恵器まで確認されている。, and it has been suggested that at least two rounds of secondary interment occurred well after the original construction小沢（2008）p.373. == Features of Kinreizuka Kofun == Among the notable features of Kinreizuka Kofun are the abundant excavated items – in particular, the gold bells from which its name is derived白石（2007）p.150. A total of 21 decorated swords were recovered from its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, one of the highest counts found among Japanese kofun白石（2007）p.150. In addition[[Category:addition]], the use of shaped stone in parts of the chamber highlights the advanced techniques employed. The significance of Kinreizuka Kofun is also evident in its scale. By the latter half of the 6th century, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun had reached its terminal phase, and outside the Kanto region, mounds exceeding 100 m in length were rare apart from royal tombs such as the {{ill|Mise Maruyama Kofun|ja|見瀬丸山古墳|1=Maruyama Kofun (Kashihara)}}. Although keyhole–shaped kofun of around 100 m were still built in the Kanto region during this time, as one of the final examples devoid of haniwa, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as one of the largest in the region白石（2007）dd.145-151、岸本（2004）dd.282-292. Furthermore, the construction conditions and the content of the burial goods suggest that the role of the Kanto region within the [[Yamato polity]] was increasing, and that the interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun – thought to be a chieftain of the Kobiki River basin – held significant status. This is also reflected in the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}}, which mention ancient maritime routes from the [[Miura Peninsula]] to the [[Bōsō Peninsula]], implying that chieftains in the Kobiki River basin near key landing sites gained considerable power by controlling vital transportation hubs白石（2007）dd.145-151. On the other hand, Kinreizuka Kofun also reveals connections with chieftains across the Kanto region. Its composite stone chamber was built using green mud slate sourced from near Nagatoro Gorge in Saitama Prefecture and is believed to have been transported via the waterways of the {{ill|Arakawa|ja|荒川 (関東)}} and [[Tokyo Bay]]. In contrast, the sandstone used in its stone chamber – quarried in the Futtsu area of Chiba – is also employed in the horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers of the {{ill|Shōgunyama Kofun|ja|将軍山古墳}} of the later period of the Saitama Kofun Group. This indicates that there was cooperation between the chieftain of the Kobiki River basin, who built Kinreizuka Kofun, and the chieftain of the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group based in present–day Futtsu City in the Koito River basin. Moreover, exchanges are suggested between the chieftains of Kazusa and those of northern Musashi who built Shōgunyama Kofun; such interactions, likely independent of direct Yamato state intervention, imply that powerful chieftains in the Kanto region from the late 6th to 7th century not only enhanced their standing within the Yamato polity but also pursued their own agendas和田（2007）dd.45-46、太田（2007）dd.97-101、木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.3. In the Bōsō region, spatial correlations between chieftains (国造) and kofun groups are observed, and the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group – including Kinreizuka Kofun – has been linked with {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. Furthermore, within the group there addears a hierarchy: chief mounds around 100 m in length, medium–sized keyhole–shaped kofun, and round kofun. The interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun, who is also considered to be {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}, stands at the apex of the chieftains in the Kobiki River basin, commanding subordinate chieftains and forging ties with leaders from the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group and other regions such as northern Musashi小沢（2007）dd.140-141、147-149、太田（2007）dd.97-101、. Some scholars also note that the prolonged period of secondary interment—suggesting that only about 4–5 individuals were interred—may be characteristic of the chieftains of the Kobiki River basin who constructed the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. == Preservation and Public Display of Excavated Items == The excavated artifacts and stone coffin from Kinreizuka Kofun were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Prior to this, in [[1956]], a Kinreizuka Relics Preservation Museum was opened in Kisarazu City. Conservation and restoration projects on the excavated items were carried out from [[1961]] to [[1963]] and from [[1989]] to [[1991]]木更津市教育委員会（2000）dd.4、14-15. Subsequently, from fiscal year 2005 onward, a large–scale reorganization project of the excavated artifacts was initiated. As a result of the reexamination of the swords, it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 21 decorated swords were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun – of which two, discovered from the passageway during the 1932 road construction, are now unaccounted for酒巻（2007）p.10. [[File:金鈴塚古墳 出土品.JPG|thumb|Exhibit at Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu (photographed June 2022)]] The excavated items from Kinreizuka Kofun are owned by Kisarazu City and are preserved and exhibited at the {{ill|Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu|ja|木更津市郷土博物館金のすず}}, which opened on October 1, [[2008]]. In addition[[Category:addition]], some items are also housed at the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}. The detailed list of excavated items designated as Important Cultural Properties is as follows. Note that after the 1959 designation, the designated names were revised in 1966, and in 2020 addition[[Category:addition]]al items were designated and the names amendedThe designation history is as follows: * In 1959 (Showa 34), the items were designated as Important Cultural Properties under the name “Kazusa Kisarazu Kinreizuka Kofun Excavated Items” (Official Notice No. 31, June 27, Showa 34). * In 1966 (Showa 41), the designated names were changed (Official Notice No. 38, June dd, Showa 41). Kinrei-tsuka Kofun Kofun
Part of the remaining posterior circular mound {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=14|frame-width=270}} | location=Nagazuka, {{ill|Kisarazu, Chiba|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}} | Position={{coord|35|23|14|N|139|55|58|E|scale:10000}} | Shape=Keyhole-shaped kofun | Dimensions=Addrox. 100 meters in length; including double moats, addrox. 140 meters in total length | BurialFacility=No-sleeve horizontal stone chamber, green schist stone sarcophagus, and wooden coffin | ConstructionEra=Late 6th century to early 7th century | BuriedPerson={{ill|Makuta Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|馬来田国造}}? | DesignatedCulturalProperty=Prefectural Historic Site | ExcavatedArtifacts=5 pure gold bells, 17 {{ill|Ornamental swords|ja|装飾付大刀}}, gilt bronze horse gear, gilt bronze ceremonial footwear, gilt bronze earrings, amber beads, {{ill|agate|ja|メノウ}} magatama, crystal beads, glass beads, mirrors, bronze bowls, iron spears, iron arrowheads, {{ill|haji ware|ja|土師器}}, and {{ill|sue ware|ja|須恵器}} | DesignationOfArtifacts=Excavated artifacts and stone sarcophagus designated as Important Cultural Property | Map2={{location map|Japan Chiba|lat_deg=35|lat_min=23|lat_sec=14|lon_deg=139|lon_min=55|lon_sec=58|label=Kinrei-tsuka Kofun|mark=前方後円墳-西南西.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kinrei-tsuka Kofun''' (金鈴塚古墳) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}} located in Nagazuka, {{ill|Kisarazu, Chiba|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}, and is part of the {{ill|Gion-Nagazuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}The Gion-Nagazuka Kofun Group is also referred to as the Gion Kofun Group or the Kisarazu Kofun Group. This article adopts the terminology used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007).. == Overview == {{Japanese Kofun |Name = Kinreizuka Kofun |image = [[File:Kinreizuka-1.jpg|250px]]
Kinreizuka Kofun Mound
A portion of the rear circular mound still remains {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=14|frame-width=270}} |Location = {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}{{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}{{ill|Nagasuka|ja|長須賀}} |Coordinates = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|23|14|N|139|55|58|E|scale:10000}} |Shape = {{ill|Keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}} |Scale = Overall mound length [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m; including its double moats, about 140 m in total |Burial facility = Sleeve‐less horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber; stone coffin made of green mud slate and a wooden coffin |Construction period = Late 6th century – Early 7th century |Interred = {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}? |Designated Cultural Property = Prefectural Historic Site |Excavated items = 5 pure–gold bells, {{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}} × 17, bronze–made horse fittings, bronze–made decorative shoes, bronze–made ear rings, an amber jujube bead, {{ill|Agate|ja|メノウ|lt=Agate magatama|lt_ja=製勾玉}}, a crystal–faceted bead, a glass bead, a mirror, a bronze vessel, an iron spear, an iron arrowhead, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土師器}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}} |Excavated items designation = The excavated items and the stone coffin have been designated as Important Cultural Properties |Map 2 = {{Location map|Japan Chiba|lat_deg=35|lat_min=23|lat_sec=14|lon_deg=139|lon_min=55|lon_sec=58|label=Kinreizuka Kofun|mark=前方後円墳-西南西.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kinreizuka Kofun''' (金鈴塚古墳) is a keyhole‐shaped kofun belonging to the {{ill|Gion‐Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}Although the group is sometimes referred to as the Gion Kofun Group or the Kisarazu Kofun Group, here the name “Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group” as used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007) is adopted. and is located in Nagasuka of {{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}. It is a keyhole‐shaped kofun. == Overview == Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole‐shaped mound with an overall length of [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m. It was once known as Nikoizuka Kofun; however, during excavations in [[1950]], five gold bells along with many other valuable artifacts were unearthed from its previously unrobbed horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, and the mound was subsequently renamed Kinreizuka Kofun in reference to the gold bells. Based on the nature of the excavated items, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered to have been constructed during the final phase of keyhole–shaped kofun, in the late 6th to early 7th century. The interred individual is believed to have been a chieftain of the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}} basin, with some attributing the identity to {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. As one of the largest keyhole–shaped kofun from the final phase, and with parts of its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber built using shaped stone, the structure employed innovative construction techniques for its time. The abundant excavated artifacts – including the gold bells and the stone coffin – were recognized for their scholarly importance and were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Furthermore, the remaining mound was designated as a Prefectural Historic Site on November 3, 1950. == Location == Kinreizuka Kofun is situated on an alluvial plain formed by the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}}, at an elevation of about 5.5 m above sea level. The plain once featured several low ridges – formerly sand dunes – and Kinreizuka Kofun was built on one such elevated spot relative to its surroundings武田（1951）dd.10-16. The area around the kofun consists of low–lying, moist land that was once mainly used for rice paddies and lotus fields; as a result, the mound eventually became utilized for land reclamation in these low–lying areas武田（1951）p.3、安藤（1998）p.14. By the end of the Meiji period the mound was recognized as a kofun and was known as Nikoizuka Kofun. At that time a small shrine venerating the kofun’s proprietor was erected on the mound by its landowner千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3. However, examination of a cadastral map drawn in April [[1876]] revealed that part of Kinreizuka Kofun had already been converted to farmland, and by the early Meiji period its original form was beginning to deteriorate武田（1951）dd.16-17. Continued land reclamation in the surrounding lowlands eventually caused most of the mound to disaddear, so that by the time of the 1950 excavation, its anterior part had almost vanished – rendering it almost circular and obscuring its original shape. After the 1950 excavation, urban development in Kisarazu further eroded the mound; the entire anterior section and part of the rear circular portion have since disaddeared, leaving only a remnant of the rear circular mound around the stone chamber, with the remainder largely replaced by residential areas. == The Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group and Kinreizuka Kofun == The {{ill|Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}, to which Kinreizuka Kofun belongs, is believed to have begun its kofun construction in the early to mid–5th century in the lower Kobiki River basin小沢（2007）p.141、白石（2007）dd.dd6-dd7. The earliest kofun in the group is estimated to be the {{ill|Takanagayachōshizuka Kofun|ja|高柳銚子塚古墳}}, with an estimated length of about 130 m; although construction paused from the late 5th to early 6th century, kofun continued to be built until the mid–7th century小沢（2007）p.141. Within this group, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as having been constructed as the last keyhole–shaped kofun during the late 6th to early 7th century. By that time, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun was drawing to a close nationwide, making Kinreizuka Kofun one of the final examples白石（2007）p.141. Within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group, a hierarchical structure existed – with large mounds about 100 m in length like Kinreizuka Kofun alongside somewhat smaller keyhole–shaped and round kofun. Thus, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered one of the chief (leader) mounds of the group. As a kofun constructed roughly contemporaneously with Kinreizuka Kofun, the {{ill|Maruyama Kofun|ja|丸山古墳}}, a keyhole–shaped mound about 70 m in length located [[Category:pp error]]approximately 700 m to the northeast, is often cited小沢（2007）p.148、小沢（2008）dd.373-374. Incidentally, after Kinreizuka Kofun was built, it is believed that a square kofun – the {{ill|Matsumen Kofun|ja|松面古墳}} – was constructed within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. The shift from keyhole–shaped to square kofun after the end of keyhole–shaped kofun construction is a trait also seen in prominent kofun groups of the Kanto region such as the {{ill|Uchizuka Kofun Group|ja|内裏塚古墳群}} in the lower reaches of the {{ill|Koito River|ja|小糸川}} in {{ill|Futtsu City|ja|富津市}} and the {{ill|Saitama Kofun Group|ja|埼玉古墳群}}. == Structure == [[File:Kinreizuka-2.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone chamber of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Based on aerial photographs taken by the US military in [[1946]], excavation results from [[1950]], and boundary surveys conducted during nearby construction from [[1998]] to [[2003]], it has been clarified that Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole–shaped mound [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m in length, with its anterior (front) portion on the west and its rear circular portion on the east. The mound is surrounded by a double moat, giving it an overall length of about 140 m木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.2、酒巻（2000）p.149. The inner moat is estimated to be about 1 m deep, while the outer moat is somewhat shallower安藤（1998）p.18. Although the mound currently stands at about 3.5 m in height, the 1950 excavation report estimated that it originally reached around 6 m based on the sediment that had flowed into the stone chamber; thus, its mound height was relatively low compared to its area武田（1951）dd.22-23、小沢（2008）p.309. Its form is thought to be two–tiered – a common feature in later–period kofun – with the first tier being relatively low with a gentle slope or serving as a platform稲木（2006）p.58. In the rear circular portion there is a horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber constructed of {{ill|Sandstone|ja|砂岩}} quarried in the Futtsu area, with its entrance facing south. The entrance opens on the second tier of the mound. The stone chamber is of the sleeve–less type, indistinguishable from its passage (【羨道】), and was restored in [[1951]] based on the 1950 excavation; its current dimensions are [[Category:pp error]]approximately 9.6 m in length, 2.2 m at its maximum width, and 2 m in height. The chamber’s profile widens gradually from its somewhat narrow entrance, then narrows slightly from the floor toward the ceiling, where a large capstone is set. However, because the entrance was cut away during road construction in [[1932]], the original precise configuration of the chamber remains unknown武田（1950）dd.25-31. Its design follows the traditional style of horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers seen in keyhole–shaped kofun in southwestern Kazusa, such as those in the Uchizuka Kofun Group in Futtsu City; yet, similarities are noted between its chamber and that of the [[Sengenyama Kofun (Sakae)|Sengenyama Kofun]] of the Ryūkakudera Kofun Group in [[Sakae, Imba District|Sakae]], Chiba – suggesting that a standardized style may have been employed in stone chamber construction in late–period keyhole–shaped kofun in the Bōsō region小沢（2008）、p.373 白井（2009)dd.21-25. == History of the Excavation == [[File:Kinreizuka-3.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone coffin of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Plans for excavating Kinreizuka Kofun had been considered since the Taishō period; however, around 1932Some sources date this to 1933 (e.g., 小沢（2008）p.398). Here, the report by the landowner published in the Chiba Prefectural Board of Education (1951) dd.17-18 is followed, dating it to around 1932. a road was built that cut into part of the remaining rear circular mound. During this construction the entrance to the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber was also cut away, leading to the discovery of bronze decorative shoes and other artifacts. Many of the major items were donated by the landowner and collected by the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}, though some materials were lost千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3、酒巻（2007）dd.10-12. After the road construction, as the mound continued to be eroded and parts of the stone chamber became exposed—raising the risk of looting—local archaeologists called for the preservation and excavation of the kofun in March 1950. Consequently, the Chiba Prefectural Historic Sites Investigation Committee, together with the Archaeological Research Laboratory of {{ill|Waseda University|ja|早稲田大学}}, conducted an excavation from April 15 to 19, 1950. When excavation began, the disaddearance and collapse of the chamber’s capstone had resulted in the interior being completely filled with sediment, so excavation was carried out from the udder part of the chamber rather than from its entrance. However, due to the unexpectedly large remaining capstone, progress was slow; the central portion of the chamber and the interior of the stone coffin were excavated first, with the remainder to be tackled later. A second excavation survey of the stone chamber was conducted from July 25 to 31, 1950, during which both the passageway at the entrance and the rear section were investigated千葉県社会教育課（1951）dd.3-7. As a result of these two rounds of excavation, an abundance of burial goods was discovered within the previously untouched stone chamber. During the July phase, five gold bells were found at the innermost part; in reference to these bells, on November 3, 1950, the kofun was designated as a historic site by Chiba Prefecture and renamed from Nikoizuka Kofun to Kinreizuka Kofun木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.4. Subsequently, during reconstruction work near the kofun in 1998, a boundary survey was conducted to ascertain its scale, and from 2000 to 2003 trenches were dug around it for further confirmation. Then, from July 28 to August 8, 2003, the remaining portion of the rear circular mound was surveyed and the stone chamber was re-excavated. These surveys confirmed that the mound measures about 100 m in length ([[Category:pp error]]approximately 140 m including its double moats) and revealed that parts of the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber were constructed using shaped stone – notably with cut stone laid on the floor – demonstrating advanced construction techniques for its time戸倉（2004）dd.32-34、41. == Excavated Items == No haniwa were found to have been used in Kinreizuka Kofun, suggesting that haniwa were not employed in its construction白石（2007）p.143; this further suddorts its classification as a late keyhole–shaped kofun. An enormous quantity of artifacts was recovered from the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber. During the 1950 excavation it was confirmed that at least three bodies were interred within the chamber – one in the central part of the stone coffin, one at its rear, and one at its front. Based on the assemblage of artifacts, it is deduced that the body at the rear of the stone coffin was interred first, followed by the one inside, and finally the body at the front. Although two pairs of ear rings were recovered from the front—suggesting that two individuals may originally have been interred there—there is no decisive evidence for multiple burials in the central and rear portions. Moreover, the relatively undisturbed state of the burial goods implies that repeated secondary interments are unlikely, and it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 4–5 individuals were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun小沢（2008）dd.309-310. From the rear of the stone coffin were unearthed the gold bells (from which the kofun takes its name), amber jujube beads, glass beads, a bronze crown, a mirror, a bronze vessel, bronze horse fittings, an iron spear, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword ({{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}}), and a large quantity of {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}}. The discovery of iron nails from the rear suggests that the body was interred in a wooden coffin. In addition[[Category:addition]], from within the stone coffin a mirror, bronze vessel, armor, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword, and bronze ear rings and glass beads were recovered, while bronze horse fittings found adjacent to the coffin are regarded as the burial goods of the interred individual. Skeletal analysis indicates that the individual in the stone coffin was a young adult male. Furthermore, from the front of the stone coffin were recovered codder vessels, bronze horse fittings, a decorated sword, crystal–faceted beads, and glass beads; bronze decorative shoes unearthed during the 1932 road construction are also considered to be associated with the individual interred at the front. The recovery of iron nails from the front confirms that this individual, too, was interred in a wooden coffin白石（2007）dd.122-127、杉山（1999）p.75. The stylistic features of the Sue pottery and decorated sword, the absence of haniwa on the mound, and the use of cut stone in parts of the chamber all indicate that Kinreizuka Kofun was constructed in the late 6th to early 7th century金鈴塚古墳の造営時期については、小沢（2008）らは6世紀末、白石（2007）は7世紀初頭とする. Furthermore, the Sue pottery exhibits a wide range of manufacturing dates酒巻（2006）によれば、金鈴塚古墳石室内で発見された須恵器の多くは6世紀末から7世紀初めのものであったが、その後に出現したタイプの須恵器も出土しており、7世紀後半に出現した須恵器まで確認されている。, and it has been suggested that at least two rounds of secondary interment occurred well after the original construction小沢（2008）p.373. == Features of Kinreizuka Kofun == Among the notable features of Kinreizuka Kofun are the abundant excavated items – in particular, the gold bells from which its name is derived白石（2007）p.150. A total of 21 decorated swords were recovered from its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, one of the highest counts found among Japanese kofun白石（2007）p.150. In addition[[Category:addition]], the use of shaped stone in parts of the chamber highlights the advanced techniques employed. The significance of Kinreizuka Kofun is also evident in its scale. By the latter half of the 6th century, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun had reached its terminal phase, and outside the Kanto region, mounds exceeding 100 m in length were rare apart from royal tombs such as the {{ill|Mise Maruyama Kofun|ja|見瀬丸山古墳|1=Maruyama Kofun (Kashihara)}}. Although keyhole–shaped kofun of around 100 m were still built in the Kanto region during this time, as one of the final examples devoid of haniwa, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as one of the largest in the region白石（2007）dd.145-151、岸本（2004）dd.282-292. Furthermore, the construction conditions and the content of the burial goods suggest that the role of the Kanto region within the [[Yamato polity]] was increasing, and that the interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun – thought to be a chieftain of the Kobiki River basin – held significant status. This is also reflected in the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}}, which mention ancient maritime routes from the [[Miura Peninsula]] to the [[Bōsō Peninsula]], implying that chieftains in the Kobiki River basin near key landing sites gained considerable power by controlling vital transportation hubs白石（2007）dd.145-151. On the other hand, Kinreizuka Kofun also reveals connections with chieftains across the Kanto region. Its composite stone chamber was built using green mud slate sourced from near Nagatoro Gorge in Saitama Prefecture and is believed to have been transported via the waterways of the {{ill|Arakawa|ja|荒川 (関東)}} and [[Tokyo Bay]]. In contrast, the sandstone used in its stone chamber – quarried in the Futtsu area of Chiba – is also employed in the horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers of the {{ill|Shōgunyama Kofun|ja|将軍山古墳}} of the later period of the Saitama Kofun Group. This indicates that there was cooperation between the chieftain of the Kobiki River basin, who built Kinreizuka Kofun, and the chieftain of the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group based in present–day Futtsu City in the Koito River basin. Moreover, exchanges are suggested between the chieftains of Kazusa and those of northern Musashi who built Shōgunyama Kofun; such interactions, likely independent of direct Yamato state intervention, imply that powerful chieftains in the Kanto region from the late 6th to 7th century not only enhanced their standing within the Yamato polity but also pursued their own agendas和田（2007）dd.45-46、太田（2007）dd.97-101、木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.3. In the Bōsō region, spatial correlations between chieftains (国造) and kofun groups are observed, and the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group – including Kinreizuka Kofun – has been linked with {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. Furthermore, within the group there addears a hierarchy: chief mounds around 100 m in length, medium–sized keyhole–shaped kofun, and round kofun. The interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun, who is also considered to be {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}, stands at the apex of the chieftains in the Kobiki River basin, commanding subordinate chieftains and forging ties with leaders from the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group and other regions such as northern Musashi小沢（2007）dd.140-141、147-149、太田（2007）dd.97-101、. Some scholars also note that the prolonged period of secondary interment—suggesting that only about 4–5 individuals were interred—may be characteristic of the chieftains of the Kobiki River basin who constructed the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. == Preservation and Public Display of Excavated Items == The excavated artifacts and stone coffin from Kinreizuka Kofun were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Prior to this, in [[1956]], a Kinreizuka Relics Preservation Museum was opened in Kisarazu City. Conservation and restoration projects on the excavated items were carried out from [[1961]] to [[1963]] and from [[1989]] to [[1991]]木更津市教育委員会（2000）dd.4、14-15. Subsequently, from fiscal year 2005 onward, a large–scale reorganization project of the excavated artifacts was initiated. As a result of the reexamination of the swords, it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 21 decorated swords were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun – of which two, discovered from the passageway during the 1932 road construction, are now unaccounted for酒巻（2007）p.10. [[File:金鈴塚古墳 出土品.JPG|thumb|Exhibit at Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu (photographed June 2022)]] The excavated items from Kinreizuka Kofun are owned by Kisarazu City and are preserved and exhibited at the {{ill|Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu|ja|木更津市郷土博物館金のすず}}, which opened on October 1, [[2008]]. In addition[[Category:addition]], some items are also housed at the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}. The detailed list of excavated items designated as Important Cultural Properties is as follows. Note that after the 1959 designation, the designated names were revised in 1966, and in 2020 addition[[Category:addition]]al items were designated and the names amendedThe designation history is as follows: * In 1959 (Showa 34), the items were designated as Important Cultural Properties under the name “Kazusa Kisarazu Kinreizuka Kofun Excavated Items” (Official Notice No. 31, June 27, Showa 34). * In 1966 (Showa 41), the designated names were changed (Official Notice No. 38, June dd, Showa 41). (※The specific details regarding swords and horse fittings have been omitted.) * In 2020 (Reiwa 2), items previously not designated were added to the Important Cultural Properties and the main name was changed from “Kazusa Kisarazu Kinreizuka Kofun Excavated Items” to “Chiba Prefecture Kinreizuka Kofun Excavated Items”, with the notation simplified (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Official Notice No. 120, September 30, Reiwa 2). * The items addition[[Category:addition]]ally designated in 2020 are as follows: ** All metal products (collectively), 1 organic product, 93 pieces of Sue pottery/Haji pottery, collectively the remnants of metal and organic products, and collectively the remnants of Sue pottery/Haji pottery. ; Chiba Prefecture Kinreizuka Kofun Excavated Items * Primary – 5 gold bells * Primary – 19 decorated swords * Primary – Metal products (collectively) * Primary – Gemstones (collectively) * Primary – Organic products (collectively) * Primary – 269 pieces of Sue pottery/Haji pottery * Primary – 1 box–type stone coffin (located within the kofun’s stone chamber) * Suddlementary – Remnants of metal and organic products (collectively) * Suddlementary – Remnants of Sue pottery/Haji pottery (collectively) ※ The above item names reflect the post–2020 revisions.Prior to the 2020 changes, the designated item details were listed as follows: : (Detailed list omitted for brevity) == Footnotes == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === Notes === === Sources === {{Reflist|2}} == References == * Chiba Prefectural Board of Education. “Kazusa Kinreizuka Kofun”. This article adopts the terminology used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007).. == Overview == {{Japanese Kofun |Name = Kinreizuka Kofun |image = [[File:Kinreizuka-1.jpg|250px]]
Kinreizuka Kofun Mound
A portion of the rear circular mound still remains {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=14|frame-width=270}} |Location = {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}{{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}{{ill|Nagasuka|ja|長須賀}} |Coordinates = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|23|14|N|139|55|58|E|scale:10000}} |Shape = {{ill|Keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}} |Scale = Overall mound length [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m; including its double moats, about 140 m in total |Burial facility = Sleeve‐less horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber; stone coffin made of green mud slate and a wooden coffin |Construction period = Late 6th century – Early 7th century |Interred = {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}? |Designated Cultural Property = Prefectural Historic Site |Excavated items = 5 pure–gold bells, {{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}} × 17, bronze–made horse fittings, bronze–made decorative shoes, bronze–made ear rings, an amber jujube bead, {{ill|Agate|ja|メノウ|lt=Agate magatama|lt_ja=製勾玉}}, a crystal–faceted bead, a glass bead, a mirror, a bronze vessel, an iron spear, an iron arrowhead, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土師器}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}} |Excavated items designation = The excavated items and the stone coffin have been designated as Important Cultural Properties |Map 2 = {{Location map|Japan Chiba|lat_deg=35|lat_min=23|lat_sec=14|lon_deg=139|lon_min=55|lon_sec=58|label=Kinreizuka Kofun|mark=前方後円墳-西南西.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kinreizuka Kofun''' (金鈴塚古墳) is a keyhole‐shaped kofun belonging to the {{ill|Gion‐Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}Although the group is sometimes referred to as the Gion Kofun Group or the Kisarazu Kofun Group, here the name “Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group” as used by Shiraishi (2007) and Ozawa (2007) is adopted. and is located in Nagasuka of {{ill|Kisarazu City|ja|木更津市}}, {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|ja|千葉県}}. It is a keyhole‐shaped kofun. == Overview == Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole‐shaped mound with an overall length of [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m. It was once known as Nikoizuka Kofun; however, during excavations in [[1950]], five gold bells along with many other valuable artifacts were unearthed from its previously unrobbed horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, and the mound was subsequently renamed Kinreizuka Kofun in reference to the gold bells. Based on the nature of the excavated items, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered to have been constructed during the final phase of keyhole–shaped kofun, in the late 6th to early 7th century. The interred individual is believed to have been a chieftain of the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}} basin, with some attributing the identity to {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. As one of the largest keyhole–shaped kofun from the final phase, and with parts of its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber built using shaped stone, the structure employed innovative construction techniques for its time. The abundant excavated artifacts – including the gold bells and the stone coffin – were recognized for their scholarly importance and were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Furthermore, the remaining mound was designated as a Prefectural Historic Site on November 3, 1950. == Location == Kinreizuka Kofun is situated on an alluvial plain formed by the {{ill|Kobiki River|ja|小櫃川}}, at an elevation of about 5.5 m above sea level. The plain once featured several low ridges – formerly sand dunes – and Kinreizuka Kofun was built on one such elevated spot relative to its surroundings武田（1951）dd.10-16. The area around the kofun consists of low–lying, moist land that was once mainly used for rice paddies and lotus fields; as a result, the mound eventually became utilized for land reclamation in these low–lying areas武田（1951）p.3、安藤（1998）p.14. By the end of the Meiji period the mound was recognized as a kofun and was known as Nikoizuka Kofun. At that time a small shrine venerating the kofun’s proprietor was erected on the mound by its landowner千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3. However, examination of a cadastral map drawn in April [[1876]] revealed that part of Kinreizuka Kofun had already been converted to farmland, and by the early Meiji period its original form was beginning to deteriorate武田（1951）dd.16-17. Continued land reclamation in the surrounding lowlands eventually caused most of the mound to disaddear, so that by the time of the 1950 excavation, its anterior part had almost vanished – rendering it almost circular and obscuring its original shape. After the 1950 excavation, urban development in Kisarazu further eroded the mound; the entire anterior section and part of the rear circular portion have since disaddeared, leaving only a remnant of the rear circular mound around the stone chamber, with the remainder largely replaced by residential areas. == The Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group and Kinreizuka Kofun == The {{ill|Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group|ja|祇園・長須賀古墳群}}, to which Kinreizuka Kofun belongs, is believed to have begun its kofun construction in the early to mid–5th century in the lower Kobiki River basin小沢（2007）p.141、白石（2007）dd.dd6-dd7. The earliest kofun in the group is estimated to be the {{ill|Takanagayachōshizuka Kofun|ja|高柳銚子塚古墳}}, with an estimated length of about 130 m; although construction paused from the late 5th to early 6th century, kofun continued to be built until the mid–7th century小沢（2007）p.141. Within this group, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as having been constructed as the last keyhole–shaped kofun during the late 6th to early 7th century. By that time, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun was drawing to a close nationwide, making Kinreizuka Kofun one of the final examples白石（2007）p.141. Within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group, a hierarchical structure existed – with large mounds about 100 m in length like Kinreizuka Kofun alongside somewhat smaller keyhole–shaped and round kofun. Thus, Kinreizuka Kofun is considered one of the chief (leader) mounds of the group. As a kofun constructed roughly contemporaneously with Kinreizuka Kofun, the {{ill|Maruyama Kofun|ja|丸山古墳}}, a keyhole–shaped mound about 70 m in length located [[Category:pp error]]approximately 700 m to the northeast, is often cited小沢（2007）p.148、小沢（2008）dd.373-374. Incidentally, after Kinreizuka Kofun was built, it is believed that a square kofun – the {{ill|Matsumen Kofun|ja|松面古墳}} – was constructed within the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. The shift from keyhole–shaped to square kofun after the end of keyhole–shaped kofun construction is a trait also seen in prominent kofun groups of the Kanto region such as the {{ill|Uchizuka Kofun Group|ja|内裏塚古墳群}} in the lower reaches of the {{ill|Koito River|ja|小糸川}} in {{ill|Futtsu City|ja|富津市}} and the {{ill|Saitama Kofun Group|ja|埼玉古墳群}}. == Structure == [[File:Kinreizuka-2.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone chamber of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Based on aerial photographs taken by the US military in [[1946]], excavation results from [[1950]], and boundary surveys conducted during nearby construction from [[1998]] to [[2003]], it has been clarified that Kinreizuka Kofun is a keyhole–shaped mound [[Category:pp error]]approximately 100 m in length, with its anterior (front) portion on the west and its rear circular portion on the east. The mound is surrounded by a double moat, giving it an overall length of about 140 m木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.2、酒巻（2000）p.149. The inner moat is estimated to be about 1 m deep, while the outer moat is somewhat shallower安藤（1998）p.18. Although the mound currently stands at about 3.5 m in height, the 1950 excavation report estimated that it originally reached around 6 m based on the sediment that had flowed into the stone chamber; thus, its mound height was relatively low compared to its area武田（1951）dd.22-23、小沢（2008）p.309. Its form is thought to be two–tiered – a common feature in later–period kofun – with the first tier being relatively low with a gentle slope or serving as a platform稲木（2006）p.58. In the rear circular portion there is a horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber constructed of {{ill|Sandstone|ja|砂岩}} quarried in the Futtsu area, with its entrance facing south. The entrance opens on the second tier of the mound. The stone chamber is of the sleeve–less type, indistinguishable from its passage (【羨道】), and was restored in [[1951]] based on the 1950 excavation; its current dimensions are [[Category:pp error]]approximately 9.6 m in length, 2.2 m at its maximum width, and 2 m in height. The chamber’s profile widens gradually from its somewhat narrow entrance, then narrows slightly from the floor toward the ceiling, where a large capstone is set. However, because the entrance was cut away during road construction in [[1932]], the original precise configuration of the chamber remains unknown武田（1950）dd.25-31. Its design follows the traditional style of horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers seen in keyhole–shaped kofun in southwestern Kazusa, such as those in the Uchizuka Kofun Group in Futtsu City; yet, similarities are noted between its chamber and that of the [[Sengenyama Kofun (Sakae)|Sengenyama Kofun]] of the Ryūkakudera Kofun Group in [[Sakae, Imba District|Sakae]], Chiba – suggesting that a standardized style may have been employed in stone chamber construction in late–period keyhole–shaped kofun in the Bōsō region小沢（2008）、p.373 白井（2009)dd.21-25. == History of the Excavation == [[File:Kinreizuka-3.jpg|thumb|200px|Stone coffin of Kinreizuka Kofun]] Plans for excavating Kinreizuka Kofun had been considered since the Taishō period; however, around 1932Some sources date this to 1933 (e.g., 小沢（2008）p.398). Here, the report by the landowner published in the Chiba Prefectural Board of Education (1951) dd.17-18 is followed, dating it to around 1932. a road was built that cut into part of the remaining rear circular mound. During this construction the entrance to the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber was also cut away, leading to the discovery of bronze decorative shoes and other artifacts. Many of the major items were donated by the landowner and collected by the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}, though some materials were lost千葉県社会教育課（1951）p.3、酒巻（2007）dd.10-12. After the road construction, as the mound continued to be eroded and parts of the stone chamber became exposed—raising the risk of looting—local archaeologists called for the preservation and excavation of the kofun in March 1950. Consequently, the Chiba Prefectural Historic Sites Investigation Committee, together with the Archaeological Research Laboratory of {{ill|Waseda University|ja|早稲田大学}}, conducted an excavation from April 15 to 19, 1950. When excavation began, the disaddearance and collapse of the chamber’s capstone had resulted in the interior being completely filled with sediment, so excavation was carried out from the udder part of the chamber rather than from its entrance. However, due to the unexpectedly large remaining capstone, progress was slow; the central portion of the chamber and the interior of the stone coffin were excavated first, with the remainder to be tackled later. A second excavation survey of the stone chamber was conducted from July 25 to 31, 1950, during which both the passageway at the entrance and the rear section were investigated千葉県社会教育課（1951）dd.3-7. As a result of these two rounds of excavation, an abundance of burial goods was discovered within the previously untouched stone chamber. During the July phase, five gold bells were found at the innermost part; in reference to these bells, on November 3, 1950, the kofun was designated as a historic site by Chiba Prefecture and renamed from Nikoizuka Kofun to Kinreizuka Kofun木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.4. Subsequently, during reconstruction work near the kofun in 1998, a boundary survey was conducted to ascertain its scale, and from 2000 to 2003 trenches were dug around it for further confirmation. Then, from July 28 to August 8, 2003, the remaining portion of the rear circular mound was surveyed and the stone chamber was re-excavated. These surveys confirmed that the mound measures about 100 m in length ([[Category:pp error]]approximately 140 m including its double moats) and revealed that parts of the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber were constructed using shaped stone – notably with cut stone laid on the floor – demonstrating advanced construction techniques for its time戸倉（2004）dd.32-34、41. == Excavated Items == No haniwa were found to have been used in Kinreizuka Kofun, suggesting that haniwa were not employed in its construction白石（2007）p.143; this further suddorts its classification as a late keyhole–shaped kofun. An enormous quantity of artifacts was recovered from the horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber. During the 1950 excavation it was confirmed that at least three bodies were interred within the chamber – one in the central part of the stone coffin, one at its rear, and one at its front. Based on the assemblage of artifacts, it is deduced that the body at the rear of the stone coffin was interred first, followed by the one inside, and finally the body at the front. Although two pairs of ear rings were recovered from the front—suggesting that two individuals may originally have been interred there—there is no decisive evidence for multiple burials in the central and rear portions. Moreover, the relatively undisturbed state of the burial goods implies that repeated secondary interments are unlikely, and it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 4–5 individuals were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun小沢（2008）dd.309-310. From the rear of the stone coffin were unearthed the gold bells (from which the kofun takes its name), amber jujube beads, glass beads, a bronze crown, a mirror, a bronze vessel, bronze horse fittings, an iron spear, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword ({{ill|Decorated Sword|ja|装飾付大刀|lt=Decorated Sword|lt_ja=飾大刀}}), and a large quantity of {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器}}. The discovery of iron nails from the rear suggests that the body was interred in a wooden coffin. In addition[[Category:addition]], from within the stone coffin a mirror, bronze vessel, armor, iron arrowheads, a decorated sword, and bronze ear rings and glass beads were recovered, while bronze horse fittings found adjacent to the coffin are regarded as the burial goods of the interred individual. Skeletal analysis indicates that the individual in the stone coffin was a young adult male. Furthermore, from the front of the stone coffin were recovered codder vessels, bronze horse fittings, a decorated sword, crystal–faceted beads, and glass beads; bronze decorative shoes unearthed during the 1932 road construction are also considered to be associated with the individual interred at the front. The recovery of iron nails from the front confirms that this individual, too, was interred in a wooden coffin白石（2007）dd.122-127、杉山（1999）p.75. The stylistic features of the Sue pottery and decorated sword, the absence of haniwa on the mound, and the use of cut stone in parts of the chamber all indicate that Kinreizuka Kofun was constructed in the late 6th to early 7th century金鈴塚古墳の造営時期については、小沢（2008）らは6世紀末、白石（2007）は7世紀初頭とする. Furthermore, the Sue pottery exhibits a wide range of manufacturing dates酒巻（2006）によれば、金鈴塚古墳石室内で発見された須恵器の多くは6世紀末から7世紀初めのものであったが、その後に出現したタイプの須恵器も出土しており、7世紀後半に出現した須恵器まで確認されている。, and it has been suggested that at least two rounds of secondary interment occurred well after the original construction小沢（2008）p.373. == Features of Kinreizuka Kofun == Among the notable features of Kinreizuka Kofun are the abundant excavated items – in particular, the gold bells from which its name is derived白石（2007）p.150. A total of 21 decorated swords were recovered from its horizontal tunnel–style stone chamber, one of the highest counts found among Japanese kofun白石（2007）p.150. In addition[[Category:addition]], the use of shaped stone in parts of the chamber highlights the advanced techniques employed. The significance of Kinreizuka Kofun is also evident in its scale. By the latter half of the 6th century, the construction of keyhole–shaped kofun had reached its terminal phase, and outside the Kanto region, mounds exceeding 100 m in length were rare apart from royal tombs such as the {{ill|Mise Maruyama Kofun|ja|見瀬丸山古墳|1=Maruyama Kofun (Kashihara)}}. Although keyhole–shaped kofun of around 100 m were still built in the Kanto region during this time, as one of the final examples devoid of haniwa, Kinreizuka Kofun is regarded as one of the largest in the region白石（2007）dd.145-151、岸本（2004）dd.282-292. Furthermore, the construction conditions and the content of the burial goods suggest that the role of the Kanto region within the [[Yamato polity]] was increasing, and that the interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun – thought to be a chieftain of the Kobiki River basin – held significant status. This is also reflected in the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}}, which mention ancient maritime routes from the [[Miura Peninsula]] to the [[Bōsō Peninsula]], implying that chieftains in the Kobiki River basin near key landing sites gained considerable power by controlling vital transportation hubs白石（2007）dd.145-151. On the other hand, Kinreizuka Kofun also reveals connections with chieftains across the Kanto region. Its composite stone chamber was built using green mud slate sourced from near Nagatoro Gorge in Saitama Prefecture and is believed to have been transported via the waterways of the {{ill|Arakawa|ja|荒川 (関東)}} and [[Tokyo Bay]]. In contrast, the sandstone used in its stone chamber – quarried in the Futtsu area of Chiba – is also employed in the horizontal tunnel–style stone chambers of the {{ill|Shōgunyama Kofun|ja|将軍山古墳}} of the later period of the Saitama Kofun Group. This indicates that there was cooperation between the chieftain of the Kobiki River basin, who built Kinreizuka Kofun, and the chieftain of the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group based in present–day Futtsu City in the Koito River basin. Moreover, exchanges are suggested between the chieftains of Kazusa and those of northern Musashi who built Shōgunyama Kofun; such interactions, likely independent of direct Yamato state intervention, imply that powerful chieftains in the Kanto region from the late 6th to 7th century not only enhanced their standing within the Yamato polity but also pursued their own agendas和田（2007）dd.45-46、太田（2007）dd.97-101、木更津市教育委員会（2000）p.3. In the Bōsō region, spatial correlations between chieftains (国造) and kofun groups are observed, and the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group – including Kinreizuka Kofun – has been linked with {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}. Furthermore, within the group there addears a hierarchy: chief mounds around 100 m in length, medium–sized keyhole–shaped kofun, and round kofun. The interred individual of Kinreizuka Kofun, who is also considered to be {{ill|Baraida Kunizukuri|ja|馬来田国造}}, stands at the apex of the chieftains in the Kobiki River basin, commanding subordinate chieftains and forging ties with leaders from the adjacent Uchizuka Kofun Group and other regions such as northern Musashi小沢（2007）dd.140-141、147-149、太田（2007）dd.97-101、. Some scholars also note that the prolonged period of secondary interment—suggesting that only about 4–5 individuals were interred—may be characteristic of the chieftains of the Kobiki River basin who constructed the Gion–Nagasuka Kofun Group. == Preservation and Public Display of Excavated Items == The excavated artifacts and stone coffin from Kinreizuka Kofun were designated as Important Cultural Properties on June 27, [[1959]]. Prior to this, in [[1956]], a Kinreizuka Relics Preservation Museum was opened in Kisarazu City. Conservation and restoration projects on the excavated items were carried out from [[1961]] to [[1963]] and from [[1989]] to [[1991]]木更津市教育委員会（2000）dd.4、14-15. Subsequently, from fiscal year 2005 onward, a large–scale reorganization project of the excavated artifacts was initiated. As a result of the reexamination of the swords, it is estimated that [[Category:pp error]]approximately 21 decorated swords were interred in Kinreizuka Kofun – of which two, discovered from the passageway during the 1932 road construction, are now unaccounted for酒巻（2007）p.10. [[File:金鈴塚古墳 出土品.JPG|thumb|Exhibit at Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu (photographed June 2022)]] The excavated items from Kinreizuka Kofun are owned by Kisarazu City and are preserved and exhibited at the {{ill|Kisarazu City Local Museum Kanenosuzu|ja|木更津市郷土博物館金のすず}}, which opened on October 1, [[2008]]. In addition[[Category:addition]], some items are also housed at the {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|ja|東京国立博物館}}. The detailed list of excavated items designated as Important Cultural Properties is as follows.
